title: Core memory reborn as plated toroids around through-glass vias
idea: Revive 1950s coincident-current ferrite core memory on 515x510 mm glass panels: laser-modified, wet-etched through-glass vias at ~3 um pitch get an electroplated square-loop NiFeMo toroid, and the X, Y and sense wires become ordinary panel redistribution layers instead of hand-threaded wire. The panel is a passive array; drivers and sense amps sit on a small CMOS chiplet at its edge.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: panel-level packaging lines cost ~1/20 of a DRAM fab per m2 and need no EUV or sub-um litho. At ~10 Mb/cm2 per layer it is far below DRAM density, so the gain is refresh-free, non-volatile, radiation-hard bits from idle substrate capacity, not leading-edge cost per bit.

title: Load-sharing magnetic matrix switch moves row decoding into package
idea: Revive the 1950s load-sharing matrix switch, the core-era decoder in which a few binary drive lines threaded through a pattern of transformers excite exactly one output: build it as coupled planar transformers in the organic package substrate so 10 binary-weighted primaries select one of 1,024 wordline-group drivers. The DRAM die keeps only local wordline drivers; global row predecode transistor trees leave the litho die.
why: Periphery ~49% of die (Fact 7): moving global decode off-die could recover ~5-10% die area and several periphery-only implant/metal masks, with the decoder made on ~$50M substrate lines instead of in a $15B fab. Risk is pulse fidelity of GHz transformer coupling.

title: Field-emitter array writes charge into an unpatterned storage film
idea: Revive the Williams tube and GE's 1970s electron-beam-addressed MOS memory (BEAMOS): a carbon-nanotube field-emitter array, each emitter with micro-deflection plates, sits ~20 um above a blank MOS storage film in sealed vacuum and writes and reads charge spots by secondary-emission contrast, regenerating them as the Williams tube did. Bit pitch is set by beam spot (~20 nm), not by lithography on the storage film.
why: Litho-bound scaling and capital (Fact 4): the storage plane needs zero critical masks and no access transistor; one emitter sweeping a 50x50 um field addresses ~6M bits, moving complexity into a coarse emitter chip and cutting the 5-7 EUV array layers to none. Latency may land at 100 ns-1 us.

title: Selectron-style binary grid stack decodes electrons without transistors
idea: Revive RCA's 1946 Selectron, which steered electrons to one storage eyelet by combinations of voltages on crossed grid bars: stack log2(N) thin perforated electrode sheets over a planar cold cathode so each sheet blocks half the windows and only the coded window passes current to its storage pad. Twenty sheets pick one of ~1M pads with 20 drivers.
why: Periphery and capital (Fact 7): decoding becomes electrostatics in vacuum with log2N wires instead of transistor trees, and the 1-5 um sheets are MEMS laminations from depreciated 150 mm lines; risk is pad density, beam crosstalk and vacuum packaging.

title: Slow-light silicon-nitride delay-line memory from depreciated photonics fabs
idea: Revive the mercury delay line as coupled-resonator slow-light silicon-nitride waveguides (group index ~50-100) made in depreciated 200 mm photonics fabs with i-line litho and 1-2 masks: 64 WDM channels at 50 Gbaud recirculate through an on-chip amplifier and retimer, and data is tapped as it passes. It serves bandwidth-hungry, capacity-poor sequential buffers such as activation staging.
why: EUV dependence and capital (Fact 4): ~2 masks on 200 mm tool sets worth ~1% of a DRAM fab, replacing leading-edge SRAM buffers; density is only ~1 Mb/cm2, so the gain is capital per unit bandwidth, not cost per bit.

title: MEMS micro-drum with a thousand heads and unpatterned media
idea: Revive the 1950s magnetic drum as a 2 mm MEMS rotor on an electrostatic or gas bearing spinning at ~1M rpm, coated with continuous perpendicular magnetic media and served by 1,000 fixed thin-film heads around its rim, so a wanted bit arrives within ~60 ns. Bits are defined by head field, so the media needs no lithography at all.
why: Capital and litho (Fact 4): heads come from mature HDD-head wafer fabs (~100 nm rules) and the rotor from 1 um MEMS lines; at ~1 Tb/in2 media density a 3 mm2 face holds ~5 Gb; risks are bearing wear, shock and rotational latency.

title: Vertical CCD strings in a 3D-NAND stack, four phase contacts
idea: Revive 1970s CCD serial memory (Fairchild F464, Intel 2416), which needed no contact or access transistor per bit, as vertical charge-coupled strings: a 3D-NAND-style alternating oxide/gate stack is etched once for channel holes, and every fourth gate layer is tied to the same clock phase so charge packets march up the hole to a sense node at the top. With only four phase lines, the staircase and per-tier contacts disappear.
why: Fact 2 and capital: one critical hole mask for ~200 tiers, no staircase (10+ masks and trims in 3D NAND) and no capacitor pillar; shifting at ~2 GHz gives ~50 ns average latency, and recirculation doubles as refresh. Risk is charge-transfer efficiency and dark current in a deposited channel liner.

title: Glass-coated microwire twistors woven into memory fabric on looms
idea: Revive Bell Labs' 1957 twistor (helically magnetized tape wound on a wire) using Taylor-Ulitovsky glass-coated CoFeSiB microwires, already drawn by the kilometre at 5-20 um diameter, given helical anisotropy by torsion annealing; an industrial loom weaves them with copper word straps into a fabric whose crossings are bits, read by giant magneto-impedance. No wafer, litho or vacuum tool touches the array.
why: Capital intensity: a microwire tower plus loom costs ~$1-5M and can run anywhere in the U.S.; density is low (~1-10 Mb/cm2 per layer), so the step change is capital per bit for a refresh-free capacity tier, not leading-edge cost per bit.

title: Goto parametrons built in BAW-filter fabs store phase bits
idea: Revive Eiichi Goto's 1954 parametron, which held a bit as the 0 or pi phase of a parametrically pumped resonator, using arrays of ScAlN micro-resonators pumped at 2f by a shared on-chip line; a bit is read by mixing with a reference phase and written by briefly injecting a seed tone. The pump sustains the state, so there is no leaking capacitor and no access-transistor tail.
why: Facts 1 and 3 plus capital: no capacitor etch and no refresh, built in 5-8 mask 150/200 mm BAW-filter fabs that ship billions of parts a year (including U.S. sites). Risks are continuous pump power and ~1 um2 resonators that leave density ~10x below DRAM unless shrunk to NEMS.

title: Tunnel-diode SRAM revived with SiGe interband diodes in contacts
idea: Revive the 1960s Esaki tunnel-diode store and TI's 1990s tunneling SRAM (one transistor plus two series negative-resistance diodes) using CVD-grown Si/SiGe resonant interband tunnel diodes stacked inside the cell contact plug, so the bistable latch sits under the bitline contact. The cell is static at near-1T area, so the capacitor module is deleted.
why: Facts 1 and 3: removes the 60-75:1 capacitor pillar (~15-20 steps including the hardest dry etch) and all refresh, at ~8-10F2 vs 6F2. Risk is valley current: it must reach ~fA per cell for standby power to beat refresh.

title: Bloch-line memory: bits smaller than the lithography defining them
idea: Revive NEC and JPL's 1980s Bloch-line memory, where bits are pairs of vertical Bloch lines inside the walls of litho-defined stripe domains, using modern ferrimagnetic garnet or PMA multilayer films and spin-orbit-torque pulses to shift the lines along the walls. Lithography only draws stripes at ~100 nm; the film's exchange length (~10 nm) sets bit pitch along each wall.
why: Litho-bound scaling (Fact 4): a ~10x density multiplier over drawn pitch, so arrays could be patterned with i-line/KrF on 200 mm tools instead of EUV. Risks are speed (historically microseconds) and Bloch-line stability at 10 nm.

title: Diode-capacitor crossbar DRAM using NiO/Ga2O3 heterojunction diodes
idea: Revive the 1950s diode-capacitor store (a rectifier per capacitor, no transistor) as a BEOL crossbar: each crossing stacks a p-NiO/n-Ga2O3 heterojunction diode (4.8 eV gap) on a MIM capacitor, written by forward-biasing the diode and read by charge sharing with a lowered row. Layers repeat at ~2 masks each above CMOS periphery.
why: Capital and Fact 2: 4F2 per layer with no FEOL array transistor and ~2 masks per stacked layer instead of 5-7 EUV layers; ultra-wide-gap reverse leakage could stretch retention ~100x (Fact 3). Risks are diode ideality and half-select disturb.

title: Vacuum-channel nano-triode as a leakage-free DRAM access switch
idea: Revive the vacuum tube at 50 nm: replace the access transistor with a vacuum-channel triode whose emitter tip and collector are separated by a ~30 nm sealed vacuum gap made by an undercut etch and gated by a surrounding electrode. A vacuum gap has no junction or GIDL path, so the capacitor leaks only through its dielectric.
why: Facts 3 and 10: off-state leakage below 1e-18 A would remove refresh (16-33% of idle power, 10-20% of bandwidth) with ~3 masks for undercut and seal. Risks are 5-10 V emission voltage, tip wear and hermetic sealing at DRAM pitch.

title: Trench-capacitor eDRAM revived inside idle U.S. logic fabs
idea: Revive IBM/Siemens/Qimonda deep-trench DRAM, abandoned by commodity DRAM in 2009 but kept in IBM POWER eDRAM down to 14 nm: license the deep-trench module to U.S. logic fabs so they can sell multi-GB memory chiplets from idle 14-28 nm capacity. The trench is formed before transistors, so it fits logic flows without a dedicated DRAM line.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: no new fab dollars and only ~4 extra masks on depreciated 300 mm logic lines; trench Cs ~20-40 fF eases refresh; density is ~3-5x below 1-beta DRAM, so the gain is fast domestic supply at low marginal capex.

title: Catt-spiral wafer-scale DRAM that routes around bad tiles
idea: Revive Anamartic's 1989 Wafer Stack, built on Ivor Catt's self-organizing spiral: every DRAM tile on an uncut wafer tests itself at power-up and links to a good neighbour, forming a chain that skips bad tiles, while a wafer-level redistribution layer brings out wide buses to a host. No dicing, die test, packaging or TSVs.
why: Fact 6 and capital: avoids HBM's ~3x area-per-bit TSV tax and 20-30% stack yield loss plus packaging and test lines (~15-25% of DRAM cost); tolerates lower yield, so depreciated 300 mm lines can make bandwidth-rich memory.

title: Compact-synchrotron X-ray proximity lithography for DRAM array layers
idea: Revive the 1990s IBM/NTT X-ray proximity lithography programme, dropped in favour of optics, with compact storage-ring sources (~1 nm wavelength) and 1:1 membrane masks at a few um gap, combined with spacer pitch division to print DRAM's periodic arrays. One ring can feed 10-20 exposure ports.
why: EUV single-supplier risk and capital (Fact 4): a ring plus several X-ray steppers built from U.S. accelerator know-how could print the 5-7 critical layers for less than the ~$200M+ per EUV scanner; risks are 1:1 mask making and overlay.

title: Vertical thyristor RAM revived inside the 4F² pillar
idea: Revive T-RAM and Kilopass's vertical-layered thyristor RAM (abandoned ~2010-2017): build a pnpn latch in the same vertical silicon pillar that 4F2 vertical-channel DRAM already etches, with a gated base for fast set and reset. The bistable thyristor holds data with a small standby current, so no storage capacitor is formed.
why: Fact 1 and capital: deletes the capacitor module (high-AR etch, high-k ALD, top plate) for ~15-20 fewer steps and about one EUV layer. Risks are standby current and temperature sensitivity.

title: Mandated U.S. second-source licensing of DRAM designs, 1970s-style
idea: Revive the 1970s-80s rule, enforced by military and big buyers, that every memory part had a licensed second source (the Intel 1103 was second-sourced): require that DRAM bought in volume by federal agencies and subsidized hyperscalers has a licensed U.S. second source, with design, test programs and process recipes transferred under royalty.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: transfers proven designs instead of each new entrant spending 5+ years of learning; could seed ~5-10% domestic supply on existing logic or legacy lines within ~3 years.

title: Core-rope weights: maskless via-programmed BEOL ROM frees HBM
idea: Revive Apollo's core-rope memory, where the wiring itself encoded the program: build generic base wafers with 8 stacked metal crossbar levels and encode a frozen model's weights only in the via layers, written maskless by multibeam e-beam, so each model ships as a ROM chiplet. Weights leave DRAM; HBM keeps only activations and KV cache.
why: Doing DRAM's job with less: static weights are ~50-80% of inference memory; 4F2 per via level x 8 levels at 40 nm metal pitch is ~DRAM-class density with no capacitor, no refresh and no per-model mask set.

title: GaN-on-silicon power fabs build wide-bandgap 1T1C memory
idea: Revive the 1980s compound-semiconductor dynamic memory experiments (GaAs/AlGaAs charge storage with very long retention) using enhancement-mode p-GaN-gate transistors as access devices: the 3.4 eV gap and heterojunction confinement can push off-current far below silicon's, with MIM capacitors added in a short BEOL. Production uses depreciated 150/200 mm GaN-on-Si power-device lines.
why: Fact 3 and capital: refresh intervals of minutes instead of 32-64 ms, made in GaN fabs (several in the U.S.) at ~1-5% of DRAM-fab capex; at 0.25-0.5 um rules density is 10-30x below DRAM, so the first use is refresh-free capacity tiers.

title: Fluidic self-assembly drops DRAM dielets into glass interposers
idea: Revive Alien Technology's 1990s fluidic self-assembly, where shaped micro-chips in a slurry settle into matching wells: dice DRAM into ~0.3 mm keyed trapezoidal dielets that self-orient into wells on a large glass interposer next to an accelerator, then wire them with one panel RDL layer. Thousands of dielets assemble in seconds without pick-and-place or TSV stacking.
why: Fact 6 and capital: replaces HBM's TSV stack (3x area per bit, 20-30% yield loss) with planar known-good dielets at ~10 um RDL pitch; an assembly bath costs <$1M versus $50M+ hybrid-bonding lines.

title: Transformer-coupled die stacking replaces TSVs, reviving IBM TROS
idea: Revive IBM's 1960s transformer read-only store, where data crossed between conductors by magnetic coupling, as inductive die-to-die links: each die in a DRAM stack carries top-metal coils that talk vertically through thinned silicon, so signals need no TSVs and power arrives by edge or wire bonds. Coils need no extra masks.
why: Fact 6: removes the TSV module (deep Si etch, liner, Cu fill, reveal; ~5-8 steps and a big yield hit) and TSV keep-out area, potentially halving HBM's area-per-bit penalty; risks are power delivery and coil area at 1-2 Tb/s per stack.

title: VLSI-Project-style consortium builds non-EUV DRAM patterning tools
idea: Revive Japan's 1976-80 VLSI Technology Research Association, where rival DRAM makers co-funded lithography and tool R&D and then competed: form a U.S. DRAM tool consortium funded per wafer start that develops e-beam projection, imprint and X-ray tools aimed at DRAM's periodic arrays, with IP pooled among members.
why: Capital intensity and EUV single-supplier risk: shares ~$2-4B of tool R&D across members and targets the 5-7 EUV layers behind depreciation's ~55% share of wafer cost.

title: Lehmann photo-electrochemical macropores etch capacitors without plasma
idea: Revive Volker Lehmann's 1990 photo-electrochemical macropore etching (studied by Siemens for trench DRAM): n-type silicon anodized in HF under backside LED illumination grows pores only where photogenerated holes reach the pore tips, giving straight pores of AR >150:1 from shallow seed pits. Dielectric and electrodes go in by nitrogen-purged ALD, so no step uses argon, helium or neon.
why: Fact 1 under the constraint: replaces the hardest Ar/He-diluted plasma etch with a ~$2-5M wet bench, and AR ~150 roughly doubles Cs or allows tighter pitch. Risk is pushing pore pitch below ~100 nm.

title: Self-ordered anodic alumina as a litho-free capacitor template
idea: Revive Keller's 1950s porous-alumina work and Masuda's 1995 two-step anodization: aluminium e-beam evaporated over the bitline layer (no Ar sputtering) is anodized in oxalic or sulfuric acid into hexagonally ordered pores at 40-60 nm pitch and >100:1 AR, registered to landing pads by a shallow imprinted pit pattern. Pores are lined by N2-purged ALD TiN/ZrO2/TiN to form capacitors.
why: Facts 1 and 4: removes the capacitor-hole SAQP/EUV patterning and the high-AR plasma etch (~2 critical layers, ~10 steps) with a room-temperature wet tool and no rare gas; AR >100 gives Cs >=8 fF. Risks are pore defects and pad registration.

title: Crystallographic KOH etching on (110) silicon for vertical trenches
idea: Revive 1970s anisotropic wet etching of (110) silicon, where KOH or TMAH attacks {110} ~100x faster than {111}, leaving atomically vertical {111} walls: align DRAM active-area and isolation trenches to <112> so a wet bath cuts 50:1 vertical walls with no plasma, using hard masks printed by LED or Talbot exposure. The crystal lattice becomes the CD reference.
why: Constraint and capital: replaces Ar/He-assisted STI and buried-wordline plasma etches with ~$1M wet benches; smooth {111} walls cut interface traps feeding the retention tail (Fact 3). Risks are a two-direction layout and lower nMOS mobility on (110).

title: Langmuir-Blodgett colloid monolayers pattern hexagonal capacitor arrays
idea: Revive Deckman's 1982 natural lithography and the 1930s Langmuir-Blodgett trough: transfer a wafer-scale monolayer of 30-40 nm silica spheres, steered into register by coarse imprinted wells over the landing pads, shrink the spheres by wet etch, evaporate a metal mesh and lift off to leave a hexagonal hole mask transferred by metal-assisted chemical etching. DRAM capacitors are already hexagonally packed, so the colloid matches the layout.
why: Fact 4 under the constraint: replaces the SAQP or EUV step for DRAM's densest layer with a ~$1M trough and wet steps, with no excimer neon and no argon etch. Risk is colloid grain boundaries, handled by sizing arrays to domains and repairing vacancies with redundancy.

title: Drawn coaxial-fibre bundles sliced into capacitor wafers
idea: Revive 1960s microchannel-plate and fibre-optic faceplate manufacturing: draw a preform of metal-core / high-k glass / metal-shell coaxial fibres in a nitrogen-purged tower, bundle and redraw three times to ~60 nm pitch, then slice the boule into 5 um wafers, each holding billions of parallel coaxial capacitors at AR ~80-100. Bond the slice to the transistor wafer so each landing pad catches several capacitors, averaging out random placement.
why: Facts 1 and 4: aspect ratio is set by slice thickness, not by etch, so AR 100+ needs no plasma, no litho and no rare gas, from ~$5-10M draw towers. Risks are metal/glass co-drawing below 100 nm and bond yield.

title: Rajchman laminated ferrite memory built on MLCC production lines
idea: Revive Jan Rajchman's 1960s RCA laminated-ferrite memory, where conductors were screen-printed between ferrite green sheets and co-fired into a solid block, on today's MLCC lines that already stack ~1,000 thin tape layers: X and Y conductors on alternate NiZn-ferrite sheets, laser-punched vias for layer selection, all fired in air. Each conductor crossing is a ferrite bit switched by coincident current.
why: Capital, scarcity and the constraint: MLCC lines make trillions of parts a year with no litho, no vacuum and no rare gas; 1,000 layers at ~1 Mb/cm2 each give ~1 Gb per cm2 of footprint at materials cost of cents. Risks are ferrite switching speed (tens of ns at small volumes) and drive current.

title: Lithium-niobate acoustic delay block streams KV cache in bulk
idea: Revive the 1950s mercury and quartz acoustic delay lines as a ~1 cm3 block of lithium niobate pulled by Czochralski in air (no argon), with a 2D array of evaporated transducers on one face launching 2-5 GHz bulk waves that reflect and recirculate; each transducer channel holds ~1-2 kbit per transit. LLM decoding reads the KV cache in fixed order every token, matching a delay line's access pattern.
why: Capital and the constraint: ~2 masks for transducers and no rare gas anywhere; 1e5-1e6 channels per block could hold ~1 Gb at >10 TB/s sequential bandwidth. Risks are GHz acoustic attenuation, transducer crosstalk and ~1-2 us worst-case latency.

title: ELTRAN porous-silicon layer transfer reuses seed wafers twentyfold
idea: Revive Canon's 1990s ELTRAN: anodize a CZ seed wafer into a double porous-silicon layer, grow 1-5 um device-grade epitaxial silicon on it in hydrogen with SiHCl3, bond it to a recycled handle with a thin conductive bond, split at the porous layer by water jet, then re-polish and reuse the seed 10-20 times. DRAM front-end steps run in the low-oxygen epi layer.
why: Scarce resources and the constraint: cuts argon-ambient CZ ingot pulling and Spruce Pine quartz crucible use per DRAM wafer by ~10-20x; low-oxygen epi can also tighten the retention tail (Fact 3). Epi reactors run on hydrogen.

title: Electroless bottom-up fill for wordlines and contacts, no sputtering
idea: Revive Brenner and Riddell's 1946 electroless plating: grow buried wordlines and bitline contacts bottom-up from a Pd-colloid-seeded floor with autocatalytic Co-B or Ni-B and a self-assembled monolayer diffusion barrier, so neither an Ar-sputtered TiN liner nor tungsten CVD is needed. The bath fills high-AR trenches without voids.
why: The constraint plus scarcity: removes argon PVD and the tungsten (China ~80%) in buried wordlines and contacts, using ~$2M baths instead of ~$10M PVD/CVD clusters. Risks are resistivity and work-function control in the buried wordline.

title: Revive BST, the abandoned gigabit-era DRAM dielectric, by N2-ALD
idea: Revive (Ba,Sr)TiO3, the k~200-300 perovskite the 1990s gigabit DRAM programmes abandoned because it could not be deposited conformally: grow it by ALD with nitrogen purge and ozone, crystallize it with a solid-state-laser spike anneal instead of a xenon flash lamp, and use SrRuO3 electrodes to suppress the interfacial dead layer. An effective k of 70-100 at 8 nm already meets Fact 1's target.
why: Fact 1 and capital: k ~70+ lets the capacitor drop from AR 60-75 to ~30, halving the hardest etch time, easing pattern collapse and deleting support-lattice steps. Risks are thin-film leakage and thermal budget.

title: Nano hemispherical-grain roughening boosts capacitor area without litho
idea: Revive the 1990s hemispherical-grain (HSG) polysilicon trick that roughly doubled 64 Mb capacitor area by seeding amorphous silicon until it beaded into grains: apply it to the walls of 3D-DRAM lateral capacitors, where there is more room, using LPCVD SiH4 seeding in H2/N2 to form 3-5 nm grains, then convert them to TiN or silicide electrodes.
why: Fact 1: 1.5-2x electrode area per footprint raises Cs without taller structures; LPCVD furnaces batch 100+ wafers on hydrogen and nitrogen with no rare gas. Risk is grain bridging in narrow gaps.

title: MITI 3D-IC laser recrystallization stacks single-crystal DRAM tiers
idea: Revive Japan's 1981-90 MITI 3D-IC programme, which made stacked single-crystal silicon by laser zone-melting through seed windows: deposit amorphous silicon for each 3D-DRAM tier and melt it with a scanned green Nd:YVO4 solid-state laser (no excimer, no neon) so it regrows epitaxially from seed holes to the tier below, giving crystalline lateral access transistors tier by tier.
why: Fact 2: single-crystal lateral transistors without a thick Si/SiGe superlattice epi and its thermal budget; solid-state lasers cost ~$1-3M and need no rare gas. Risks are heat reaching lower tiers and grain boundaries far from seeds.

title: Dolan-bridge angled evaporation forms self-aligned sub-litho features
idea: Revive Dolan's 1977 suspended-resist-bridge shadow evaporation, used to make Josephson junctions: one coarse imprint forms a resist bridge, and two evaporations at opposite angles in high vacuum (oxidation in O2, no argon milling) deposit overlapping strips whose overlap width is set by angle and bridge height rather than litho. Use it for ~10 nm gate-to-contact overlaps and narrow metal strips.
why: Fact 4: turns a high-resolution litho layer into a coarse layer plus geometry, removing EUV or immersion passes on self-aligned structures; e-beam evaporators cost ~$1-2M and need no rare gas. Risks are throughput and step coverage.

title: Brody-style stencil metallization replaces litho for DRAM top metals
idea: Revive T. Peter Brody's 1973 first active-matrix display, built without photolithography by evaporating each layer through aligned metal shadow masks: deposit DRAM's coarse upper metals, pads and redistribution (>=1-3 um) by thermal or e-beam evaporation through reusable silicon-nitride stencils. Each stencil serves thousands of wafers, with no resist, develop, etch or argon sputter.
why: Fact 4 and capital: removes ~4-6 of DRAM's ~50-60 mask passes with their tracks, scanners and etchers (~10% of litho spend); evaporation needs only vacuum. Risks are stencil clogging and alignment at 300 mm.

title: SCALPEL electron projection prints DRAM arrays without EUV or neon
idea: Revive Bell Labs' 1990s SCALPEL, which projected a 4x-reduced image of a scattering-contrast membrane mask with 100 keV electrons: modern high-brightness cathodes, aberration-corrected optics and fast resists let it expose DRAM's repetitive array layers in vacuum. Its source is a hot cathode, so there is no excimer neon and no EUV drive-laser helium.
why: Fact 4 under the constraint: replaces 5-7 EUV layers with tools targeted at ~$30-50M versus $200M+ for EUV. Risks are space-charge blur and throughput (~20-40 wafers/hour).

title: Talbot self-imaging with solid-state deep-UV lasers prints periodic arrays
idea: Revive Talbot's 1836 self-imaging effect: a periodic mask under coherent light reproduces itself at fixed distances, and averaging over one Talbot period (displacement Talbot) prints half-pitch features with nearly unlimited depth of focus. Use a 193-213 nm all-solid-state frequency-multiplied laser, with no ArF excimer and no neon buffer gas, for DRAM capacitor and active-area grids.
why: Fact 4 under the constraint: a lens-free proximity tool at ~$5-10M versus ~$60M immersion scanners for periodic layers, with free pitch halving. Risks are solid-state DUV power and defects in regular arrays.

title: Hydrogen-ion projection exposes straight capacitor holes, no plasma etch
idea: Revive the 1990s-2000s European ion projection lithography, which pushed helium ions through stencil masks, using protons from a hydrogen source instead: 100-200 keV protons cross ~2 um of resist with almost no lateral scatter, so stencil projection exposes capacitor holes at AR >100 directly in a thick resist mold that ALD then fills.
why: Fact 1 under the constraint: aspect ratio is set by proton range rather than plasma etch, and no helium source is used; exposure plus development replaces the hardest etch. Risks are stencil heating and resist sensitivity.

title: Solid-source diffusion and laser melt anneal replace ion implanters
idea: Revive pre-1975 diffusion doping: spin-on or ALD dopant glasses (B, P, As oxides) patterned by the existing masks are driven in by nanosecond green-laser melt anneal, giving abrupt shallow junctions without ion implanters, argon-purged beamlines or xenon flash lamps. Conformal dopant films also dope 3D sidewalls that tilted implants cannot reach.
why: Capital and the constraint: replaces ~10-15 implanters per DRAM line (~$5-10M each) and flash annealers with spin/ALD tools; conformal sidewall doping helps 3D DRAM (Fact 2). Risks are dose control and junction-leakage tails.

title: Vertical plated-wire memory: NiFe-lined holes through word-plane stack
idea: Revive 1960s plated-wire memory (NiFe electroplated on beryllium-copper wire, non-destructive readout, flown in Apollo-era and Skylab systems): etch vertical holes through an epitaxial stack of heavily doped silicon word planes by metal-assisted chemical etching, electroplate a circumferentially magnetized NiFe film on each hole wall around a copper core, and store a bit where each word plane crosses a hole. A word current tilts the magnetization slightly and the core senses the induced voltage without destroying it.
why: Facts 2 and 8: a 3D array from one critical hole mask using only aqueous etch and plating (no rare gas), with readout that avoids destructive read and writeback. Risks are mV-level read signal below 100 nm and word-plane selectivity.

title: Bubble-memory chevron ratchets driven by one global rotating field
idea: Revive 1970s bubble memory's key trick, a global rotating in-plane field that moves every domain one step per cycle along permalloy chevrons: nanoimprint asymmetric pinning chevrons into e-beam-evaporated Co/Pt or ferrimagnetic multilayers (no argon sputtering) and drive all tracks with a GHz rotating field from two crossed package striplines. No per-track transistor or current is needed; only read and write heads sit at the loop ends.
why: Fact 4 and capital: one imprint plus two coarse metal masks define the array, with no EUV and no rare gas; a major/minor-loop layout with 64-bit minor loops stepping ~1 ns gives ~50 ns access. Risks are GHz field strength and domain stability below 50 nm.

title: Zuse relay storage reborn as bistable buckled-nanobeam memory
idea: Revive the relay storage of Konrad Zuse's 1941 Z3, which held its memory in ~1,400 latching relays, as pre-buckled nanobeams with two stable shapes that snap between states under an electrostatic pulse and are read capacitively without ever touching a contact. Beams are released with vapour HF and sealed in vacuum, so the cell's off state is an empty gap.
why: Fact 3 under the constraint: mechanical bistability has no leakage tail and needs no refresh, and non-contact snapping avoids wear; ~4 BEOL masks with no rare gas, ~10 ns switching. Risks are cell size (~20-30F2) and beam fatigue at 1e15+ cycles.

title: Crowe persistent-current cells in YBCO at 77 K, no helium
idea: Revive the 1957 Crowe cell and Buck's cryotron, where a bit is a supercurrent circulating clockwise or counterclockwise in a superconducting loop, using YBCO films grown by reactive thermal co-evaporation (no argon sputtering, no KrF excimer) and cooled by liquid nitrogen made from air. A persistent current does not decay, so cells never refresh.
why: The constraint and Fact 3: liquid nitrogen replaces helium cryogenics, and loop arrays need ~4-6 masks at 0.5 um on depreciated fabs. Risks are loop inductance capping density at ~10-100 Mb/cm2 and YBCO junction reproducibility.

title: Plasmonic contact printing with UV LEDs and disposable masks
idea: Revive 1970s contact printing, abandoned because masks wore out, with two 2026 fixes: each wafer gets a disposable conformal mask nanoimprinted from a master, and a 365 nm UV-LED source excites surface plasmons in the mask's silver layer so near-field exposure resolves ~22 nm half-pitch. No laser gas and no mercury-lamp argon or xenon fill is involved.
why: Fact 4 under the constraint: ~$2-5M tools versus ~$60M immersion or $200M+ EUV for DRAM's periodic layers. Risks are contact defects, overlay and the ~20 nm plasmonic depth of field.
